title: An evaluation of the evidence that methamphetamine abuse causes cognitive decline in humans

claims.statement: In five adults from a treatment programme who were scanned after about 3 months of abstinence and again after about 14 months, striatal dopamine transporter availability rose by 19% in the caudate and 16% in the putamen; in the same programme, people abstinent for a similar time (n=10) did not differ significantly from controls, whereas those in short abstinence (n=12) were 21–26% lower. The five who stayed abstinent started with higher transporter levels than those who dropped out, no control group was rescanned, and another PET study found no relation between abstinence duration and transporter levels.
claims.magnitude: Within-person: +19% caudate, +16% putamen (n=5). Cross-sectional: protracted abstinence 5% (caudate) and 9% (putamen) below controls, not significant (n=10 vs 11; editors' standardized difference about −0.3 and −0.6, so a moderate remaining difference is not excluded); short abstinence 26% and 21% below.

claims.statement: In five people from the same treatment programme rescanned after 12–17 months of abstinence, relative thalamic glucose metabolism rose by 12% (SD 9%) while striatal metabolism did not change and remained lower than in controls; no control group was rescanned, and the reported test statistics contain errors.
claims.magnitude: Thalamus +12% (SD 9%); striatum +2.7%; occipital +0.4% (n=5). Thalamus vs controls: 1.11 vs 1.31 (short abstinence), 1.23 vs 1.31 (protracted; reported as not different).

claims.statement: Average test scores of groups of people who use methamphetamine mostly fall in the low-average to average range of population norms, and a minority of users meet conventional impairment criteria, more often than controls: about 7 of 27 users versus 2 of 18 controls met a 2-SD criterion in at least one domain in one study, and 34% of users versus 16% of controls were classified as globally impaired in another.
claims.magnitude: Group means between about the 16th and 55th percentiles on normed tests (Simon et al., 2010); impaired in at least one domain 7/27 (26%) vs 2/18 (11%) (Kalechstein et al., 2003, as reported by Hart et al., 2012); globally impaired 34% vs 16% (Iudicello et al., 2010).

claims.statement: Whether test performance improves with abstinence beyond practice effects is not established. In the two studies that retested a control group, users did not improve significantly more than controls over about a month (composite change 0.14 vs 0.00 SD, p=0.33; 18 users, 21 controls) or about a year (group-by-time interaction p=0.13; 25 abstinent users, 58 who kept using, 38 controls); a subgroup of 6 abstinent users impaired at baseline improved more, but so did 6 controls impaired at baseline. Across cross-sectional studies, length of abstinence did not moderate the size of group differences, and few studies tested people abstinent for more than a year.
claims.magnitude: Simon et al. (2010): composite change 0.14 (users) vs 0.00 (controls), t(37)=−1.01, p=0.33; editors' standardized difference in change about 0.32 (95% CI −0.31 to 0.96), so a moderate improvement is not excluded either. Iudicello et al. (2010): all groups improved (time F(1,118)=55.12); group × time p=0.126; abstainer–control gap 3.0 T at baseline, 2.7 T at follow-up. Cao et al. (2026): g −0.70 (<1 month), −0.63 (1–12 months), −0.88 (>12 months; 7 studies), p=0.33.

claims.statement: Non-using biological siblings of people with stimulant dependence share some fronto-striatal brain-structure differences and poorer inhibitory control with their dependent siblings, which indicates that some differences observed in people who use stimulants predate drug use; most dependent participants in that study used cocaine rather than methamphetamine.

Whether methamphetamine use causes lasting cognitive impairment in humans has not been established: users score lower than non-users on average, but no study has measured cognition before use began, groups differ in education and other risk factors, and the differences have not been shown to change with abstinence more than practice effects do.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable from current designs; the size of the association is given in the claim on group differences (section 9).
